author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A monthly Manchester grocery-price snapshot found a relatively quiet September shopping trip, with three tracked products declining and two increasing. The basket’s total cost was 0.23% above August and 3.25% higher than the column’s first trip in April 2025.

Manchester Ink Link emphasized that the exercise follows one shopper’s recurring list at one store and is not a scientific measure of statewide food inflation. In the September sample, avocados, mandarin oranges and fat-free milk declined, while a favorite ice cream and a bag of dry cat food increased.

The larger concern is what may happen after a new 50% tariff on Canadian imports. The report identified wood pulp used in paper goods, packaging, dairy inputs and equipment for maple producers as areas where higher import costs could eventually reach New Hampshire shoppers and businesses.

Because those effects were not yet visible in the September trip, the current figures should be read as a dated local snapshot rather than a forecast. The next monthly comparison will offer an early check on whether tariff-related costs are beginning to appear on store shelves.
dek: A Manchester price-tracking column found only five changes in its monthly basket, while warning that new Canadian tariffs could raise packaging and input costs.
headline: New Hampshire grocery snapshot tracks small September rise before tariff effects
